clips.text: Atrioventricular block means delayed or failed conduction from atria to ventricles. The problem can occur in the A V node or farther down in the His-Purkinje system. Track atrial and ventricular activity separately. Count P waves as well as Q R S complexes, and compare their timing. The phrase heart block does not mean that a coronary artery is blocked, and it does not tell us the anatomical level by itself.

clips.text: First-degree A V block is prolonged atrioventricular conduction: the P R interval is longer than zero point two zero seconds in adults, and every atrial impulse still conducts. It is a delay rather than an intermittent dropped beat. Identify the underlying rhythm, for example sinus rhythm with first-degree A V block. Q R S duration may be narrow or wide depending on other conduction findings. A prolonged P R does not automatically establish normal cardiac output.

clips.text: In the classic Mobitz one pattern, P R intervals progressively lengthen until a P wave is not followed by a Q R S complex. The sequence then repeats. This creates grouped beating and is often called Wenckebach. The block is commonly within the A V node, but exceptions exist. A narrow Q R S is common, not mandatory. Verify the pattern across enough beats instead of labeling any irregular rhythm with a dropped complex as Wenckebach.

clips.text: In Mobitz two, an occasional P wave fails to conduct despite a stable sinus rate, with unchanged P R intervals before and after the nonconducted P wave. It reflects conduction failure in the His-Purkinje system, and Q R S complexes are often wide, though they can be narrow. A two-to-one pattern alone cannot distinguish Mobitz one from Mobitz two, because there are not consecutive conducted beats to show progressive P R change. Describe it as two-to-one A V block unless additional evidence resolves the type.

clips.text: In complete, or third-degree, A V block, atrial impulses do not conduct to the ventricles. When an escape rhythm is present, atrial and ventricular activation proceed independently. An escape rhythm may be slow, unreliable, or absent. P to P and R to R intervals may each be regular, but there is no consistent P R relationship. The escape rate and Q R S width depend on the focus and conduction system. A V dissociation alone is not always proof of complete block; the full pattern matters.

clips.text: Compare four patterns. A long constant P R with every P conducted suggests first-degree delay. Progressive P R lengthening followed by a nonconducted P suggests Mobitz one. Sudden nonconducted P waves with constant conducted P R intervals suggest Mobitz two when the pattern supports that diagnosis. Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms raise concern for complete block. Give the evidence, acknowledge limitations, and follow the course's escalation expectations rather than selecting a treatment in this lesson.
